opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the nice thing is that these two aren't really separate worlds. If you look at a standard on-policy RL setup, the student model generates samples, you score them, and you update the model on its own samples. On-policy distillation has exactly the same structure. The only real difference is where the signal comes from. In RL you get a scalar reward, often just at the end of the sequence: did you get the math problem right or not. In distillation you have a teacher that gives you a dense, per-token signal: how likely would the teacher have been to produce this token in this context?

So if you already have RL infrastructure (rollout workers, a trainer, a reward model or verifier sitting somewhere), you can basically swap the reward model for a teacher model. Instead of returning one number per sequence, the teacher returns log-probs for each token the student sampled, and you use something like a reverse KL between student and teacher as a per-token reward or advantage. That was a big part of the motivation behind some of our earlier work on generalized knowledge distillation: train on the student's own generations, not just on fixed teacher outputs, so you fix the train-test mismatch the same way RL does.

Once you see it that way, combining them is pretty natural. You can have a loss that's a weighted mix: the sparse task reward from a verifier plus a dense distillation term from the teacher. Early in training, the teacher signal does a lot of the work. It's much more sample-efficient because you get feedback on every token rather than one bit per rollout. As the student gets better, you can lean more on the actual reward, especially if you want the student to eventually surpass the teacher on the task you care about.

There are some practical things you have to think about. The teacher is usually bigger, so the scoring cost is non-trivial, though it's a forward pass, not generation, so it's cheaper than you'd expect. Tokenizer mismatches between teacher and student can be annoying. And you have to choose your divergence carefully. Reverse KL is mode-seeking, which tends to be what you want for a smaller student that can't cover everything the teacher does.

But the high-level takeaway is that distillation can be a reward function. If your RL stack is reasonably modular, you get on-policy distillation almost for free, and in a lot of settings it's a much cheaper way to get the same gains you'd otherwise chase with long, expensive RL runs.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a weighted mix of verifier task reward and a dense teacher distillation signal, retaining the reward objective.

r002.rationale: It explains that on-policy distillation uses the same structure as RL: the student generates samples, which are then scored and used for updates.

r003.rationale: It proposes swapping the reward model for a teacher that supplies token log-probabilities, but does not say to replace the SFT policy as the source of logits.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that distillation and RL are actually much closer than people usually assume, and once you see that, it becomes pretty natural to run both through the same machinery.

If you look at what an RL setup gives you today, you have a policy that generates samples, you have some mechanism to score those samples, and you have a trainer that updates the policy based on those scores. That's the skeleton. Now the standard view of distillation is supervised fine-tuning on teacher outputs, which looks like a completely different pipeline. But if you do on-policy distillation, where the student generates its own samples and the teacher just scores them, you suddenly have the exact same shape. The student is the policy, the teacher's log-probs are the reward, or really a dense, per-token reward, and the trainer does what it already does.

So the mental shift is: the teacher is just another reward model. Instead of a verifier saying yes or no at the end of a trajectory, the teacher gives you a signal at every token, something like the KL between the student and the teacher on the student's own samples. And that fixes the big weakness of classic SFT distillation, which is the train-test mismatch. The student only ever sees teacher trajectories, and then at inference it drifts off that distribution and has no idea how to recover. On-policy distillation puts the student's own mistakes in the training data, with a teacher telling it how bad each step was.

The practical thing I like is that this reuses the infrastructure almost for free. You already have a generation engine, you already have a scoring side, you already have the optimizer loop. You add one more scoring path, which is running the teacher forward on the student's samples, and that's it. And then you get a lot of knobs that fall out naturally. You can mix the dense teacher signal with sparse verifiable rewards on math or code problems. You can anneal from mostly teacher to mostly environment reward. You can even use the teacher early on as a curriculum, basically to get the student into the regime where RL rewards are non-zero often enough to learn from, because pure RL on hard problems has that cold-start problem where you sample a thousand times and get nothing right.

The other thing worth saying is efficiency. RL is expensive mostly because the reward is sparse and you need a lot of samples to get a useful gradient. Dense per-token signal from a teacher is dramatically more sample efficient. So in a lot of cases you can get most of the way to the teacher's capability with a tiny fraction of the compute of RL from scratch, and then spend your RL budget on the part where the student actually needs to exceed the teacher, or go where no teacher exists.

So the short version: don't think of them as two pipelines. Think of RL as the general framework, and distillation as a particular choice of reward that happens to be dense and cheap, and build so that you can swap or blend reward sources inside one loop.

r001.rationale: The response says to use distillation as a dense teacher-derived reward within the RL loop and describes blending it with environment rewards.

r002.rationale: It explains that RL infrastructure already generates samples from the student, enabling on-policy distillation by scoring those samples with the teacher.

r003.rationale: The response describes running the teacher on student samples for scoring, but does not identify replacing the SFT policy with a larger teacher as the source of logits.

astra-6.text:
I think of distillation as another learning signal you can plug into the RL loop. You already have infrastructure that generates trajectories, scores them, and updates a policy. If you have a stronger teacher, you can use its feedback on those same trajectories to help train the student.

The interesting choice is where that feedback comes in. You could have the teacher generate demonstrations, or you could let the student generate and have the teacher guide it on the states it actually visits. I like the latter because it addresses a distribution mismatch: the student needs to learn what to do when it makes its own mistakes, not just imitate a successful teacher trajectory.

Then you can combine that distillation signal with the reward signal. The teacher gives you more detailed guidance, while reinforcement learning lets you optimize for the outcome you actually care about. They’re complementary, and much of the machinery can be shared.

r001.rationale: It says the teacher’s distillation signal can be combined with the reward signal, with RL optimizing for the desired outcome.

r002.rationale: It mentions shared RL machinery and student-generated trajectories, but does not clearly state that existing infrastructure supports distillation because it already samples from the student model.

r003.rationale: It does not identify replacing the SFT policy’s logits with logits from a larger teacher model as the proposed change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of reinforcement learning and distillation as complementary parts of the same loop. RL gives you a way to improve a policy using a reward signal, while distillation lets you transfer useful behavior from another policy. Within an existing RL stack, a natural way to combine them is to add a teacher signal alongside the reward objective.

For example, you can sample trajectories from the student, evaluate those trajectories with the teacher, and train the student to match the teacher’s token distributions on the states the student actually visits. That matters because the student will make different mistakes and reach different states than the teacher would. You can then combine that distillation loss with your policy-gradient loss.

The infrastructure is largely shared: you already have rollout generation, model inference, and a training loop. The additional piece is getting teacher feedback into that loop. The interesting question becomes how much to trust the teacher versus the reward signal. Distillation can provide a dense learning signal, while RL gives the student room to discover behavior beyond what the teacher demonstrates.

r001.rationale: It says to add a teacher signal alongside the reward objective and combine distillation loss with the policy-gradient loss.

r002.rationale: It describes sampling student trajectories and notes that rollout generation is already part of the existing infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It mentions teacher feedback and teacher token distributions, but does not specify replacing the SFT policy with a larger teacher as the source of logits.
